2027-07-14.title: Wednesday of the Fifteenth Week in Ordinary Time · St Camillus de Lellis
readings: Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground
The Lord works vindication and justice for all who are oppressed
You have hidden these things from the wise and have revealed them to infants
2027-07-14.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 15 (Year I). The first reading is the burning bush; the Mass of the weekday may be replaced by the optional memorial of St Camillus de Lellis, priest and founder, the patron of the sick, of hospitals and of nurses (white). The Lectionary leaves out verses 7–8 of Exodus 3, the heart of the passage, and they are quoted below. Liturgical colour: green (white if the memorial is kept).
2027-07-14.verse: Then he said, “Come no closer! Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground.” He said further, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.”
theo: Forty years have gone by since Moses fled from Egypt. He is now a shepherd in Midian, looking after the sheep of his father-in-law Jethro, and he has led the flock “beyond the wilderness” to Horeb, “the mountain of God.” He is an old man doing the humblest work; the prince of Egypt has become a herdsman, and it is to the herdsman that God appears. “The angel of the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire out of a bush; he looked, and the bush was blazing, yet it was not consumed.” Notice what Moses does: “I must turn aside and look at this great sight.” The whole story turns on that small decision. “When the Lord saw that he had turned aside to see, God called to him out of the bush, ‘Moses, Moses!’ And he said, ‘Here I am.’” God speaks only to someone who stops. Then come two commands that shape all worship: “Come no closer! Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground.” Ground becomes holy because God is present in it. And God names himself, not first by power but by relationship: “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Moses hides his face. The Lectionary skips two verses, and they are the heart of it: “I have observed the misery of my people who are in Egypt; I have heard their cry on account of their taskmasters. Indeed, I know their sufferings” (Exodus 3:7). The holy God is the God who sees suffering, hears the cry, and knows it from the inside. And so he sends Moses. Moses objects: “Who am I?” and God answers, not with a list of Moses' strengths, but with himself: “I will be with you.” The psalm sings it: “The Lord works vindication and justice for all who are oppressed. He made known his ways to Moses.”

In the Gospel Jesus bursts into thanksgiving: “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and the intelligent and have revealed them to infants.” The passage comes right after he has grieved over the towns that saw most and turned least, and the contrast is deliberate: those who thought they knew did not see, and the little ones did. “Infants” (Greek nepioi) are the unlearned, the humble, those with nothing to defend. The Bible has many of them: a shepherd at a bush, a boy David, fishermen from Galilee. St Paul would write that God chose “what is low and despised in the world” (1 Corinthians 1:28). Then Jesus lifts the veil on his own mystery: “All things have been handed over to me by my Father; and no one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.” This is the most intimate sentence in the first three Gospels; it sounds like the Gospel of John. Jesus is not only a messenger of God: he knows the Father as only a Son can, and he opens that knowledge to those he chooses, and he chooses the humble. The burning bush and this prayer fit together. At the bush God revealed his name and his compassion to a shepherd; in Jesus the Father reveals his whole heart to those who come like children. And the holy ground is no longer only a mountain in Sinai: it is wherever the Son is, and wherever the least of his brothers and sisters are found.
outline: Ask: when did you last stop, turn aside and look at something that you did not understand?
God speaks to the one who stops; the shepherd at the bush.
Remove your sandals: God's presence makes every place holy, and he knows our sufferings.
The Father reveals himself to the humble through the Son.
A sickbed is holy ground, and the sick are Christ himself.
live: Choose one moment today, on a bus, in the kitchen or at the roadside, to stop completely for two minutes, put the phone away and be quiet before God.
Visit or phone someone who is ill. When you enter their room, treat it as holy ground: sit, listen, and do not hurry.
saints: Born at Bucchianico in Italy, he became a soldier, a gambler and a restless young man with an incurable wound on his leg. In Rome he was treated, and then worked, in a hospital for incurables, and a sermon in 1575 turned his life round. He later founded the Ministers of the Sick, the Camillians, who wear a red cross on their habit, and he asked them to care for the sick with the love of a mother for her only child. He cared for the sick in plague and in war, and is the patron of the sick, of hospitals and of nurses. He died in Rome on 14 July 1614 and was canonised in 1746.
2027-07-14.prayer: Lord God, you appeared to Moses in the burning bush and said: I have heard the cry of my people and I know their sufferings. Make us people who turn aside to look, who take off their sandals before holy ground, and who see in every sickroom a place where your Son is present. Father, Lord of heaven and earth, we thank you that you reveal yourself to the little ones. Through the intercession of St Camillus, give strength and tenderness to all who nurse the sick, healing to those who suffer, and to each of us the knowledge that you are with us. Amen.
altar: In the Mass we, too, take off our sandals in our own way: we bow, we kneel, we are silent before the altar, because the ground of the church is holy ground. The Lord who spoke from the bush now comes in bread and wine. In the Eucharist the Son gives us the knowledge of the Father that he promised in today's Gospel. And the same Christ who is present on the altar is present, in another way, in the sick person we are asked to visit; that is why the Church has always joined the Mass to the care of the sick.

quick: Moses, a shepherd in Midian, turns aside to look at a bush that burns and is not consumed; God calls him by name and tells him to remove his sandals.
God says: I have seen my people's misery and heard their cry; I will send you, and I will be with you.
Jesus thanks the Father for revealing his secrets to infants and speaks of the knowledge between the Father and the Son.
2027-07-14.action: Visit, call or pray for someone who is ill today, and treat the moment as holy ground.
2027-07-14.question: When did I last stop, turn aside and make room for God to speak?
kidsaint: Camillus was tall and strong, and when he was young he was a soldier. One day he hurt his leg badly, and the wound would not heal. He went to a hospital in Rome, and there he saw how lonely and uncared for the sick were. He decided to spend his life nursing them. He started a group of brothers, called the Camillians, who wear a red cross, and he is said to have told them: put more heart into those hands. When you help someone who is ill, you help Jesus.

family.explain: Moses was looking after sheep when he saw something strange: a bush on fire that did not burn up! He went closer to look, and God called his name: Moses, Moses! God said: take off your sandals, because this is holy ground. God told Moses that he had seen how his people were suffering and that he would send Moses to help them. Moses was afraid, but God said: I will be with you. God is always with us, too, especially when we are helping someone who is hurting.
family.intention: We pray for sick people, for doctors and nurses, and for all who look after them. We thank God that he is always with us.
family.ask: Ask: “Who do we know who is sick? What could we make or bring, or what could we say, to cheer them up this week?”

illus: A senior nurse in a government hospital in Kerala trained her new nurses with one rule. When you enter a ward, she told them, say good morning to the patient before you look at the chart. The patient is not a case, she said; the patient is a person standing on holy ground. A young nurse later said that she did not understand the rule until a frightened old man in the bed grasped her hand and said: thank you for seeing me. The nurse added that she never forgot that the chart can wait for ten seconds. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: Lord God, you who see the sufferings of your people, turn us aside to see what you show us, and take away our fear. Amen.
share: I must turn aside and look at this great sight (Exodus 3:3). What would help me to stop and notice God in my day?
Remove the sandals from your feet (Exodus 3:5). Where do I need to approach God, or my neighbour, with more reverence?
You have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to infants (Matthew 11:25). In what ways has God taught me through the humble and the little?
pm.resp: The Lord works vindication and justice for all who are oppressed.
interc: For all who are sick, especially the dying, that they may know the nearness of Christ.
For doctors, nurses, chaplains and caregivers, that they may serve with St Camillus' tenderness.
For those who suffer in silence and whom no one visits.
For the Church, that she may always be a place of welcome for the little and the poor.
For our group, that we may turn aside, listen and answer: Here I am.
pm.close: Father, you saw the misery of your people and sent Moses to deliver them. Send us to all who suffer, and be with us as you promised. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, imagine Moses at the end of a long ordinary day. He is eighty years old, with the sheep, in the desert. Nothing special is happening. And then he sees a bush that burns and does not burn up. He could have walked on. A lot of us walk on. But Moses says: I must turn aside and look at this great sight (Exodus 3:3). And when the Lord saw that he had turned aside to see, God called to him: Moses, Moses! (Exodus 3:4). God does not shout; he waits for someone who stops.

Then God says: Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground (Exodus 3:5). It is just a patch of desert, and it is holy because God is there. When we enter a church we feel it. But God's holy ground is also the sickroom, the kitchen where someone is crying, the hospital bed. And hear what God says in the verses we did not read: I have observed the misery of my people; I have heard their cry; I know their sufferings (Exodus 3:7). Our God is no distant ruler. He knows suffering from the inside, and in his Son he entered it.

That is why St Camillus saw what he saw. A soldier with a wound that would not heal, he lay in a hospital and saw how the poor sick were treated, and he said: this is holy ground. He gave his life to nursing the sick, because Jesus himself said: I was sick and you took care of me (Matthew 25:36). Moses asked: who am I? God answered: I will be with you (Exodus 3:12). That is the only answer any of us needs when we are afraid to help.

And Jesus thanks the Father today that these things are revealed not to the wise and learned but to infants (Matthew 11:25). You do not need a degree to meet God. You need the heart of a child, which stops, looks and says: Here I am. Let us turn aside today and ask for that heart. Amen.
kids: Children, Moses was looking after the sheep one day when he saw a bush on fire, but the bush was not burning up! He went to have a look. And God called: Moses! Moses! God said: take off your sandals, this is holy ground. Then God told him: I have seen my people hurting, and I will send you to help them. Moses was afraid, but God said: I will be with you. A man called Camillus knew that God is with sick people. He looked after them with all his heart. When we are kind to someone who is sick, we are standing on holy ground too.

intro: A shepherd who turns aside, holy ground that is a sickroom, and the Father who reveals himself to infants.

sub: God speaks to the one who stops.
q: Then Moses said, “I must turn aside and look at this great sight, and see why the bush is not burned up.” When the Lord saw that he had turned aside to see, God called to him out of the bush, “Moses, Moses!” And he said, “Here I am.”
When Moses saw it, he was amazed at the sight; and as he approached to look, there came the voice of the Lord:
points.apply: Find two quiet minutes today to stop, turn aside and say to God: Here I am.

sub: Ground made holy by God's presence.
q: Then he said, “Come no closer! Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground.”
Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?
points.apply: Be reverent this week in church, and also in the home and the sickroom, because God is present in them.

q: Out of the mouths of babes and infants you have founded a bulwark because of your foes, to silence the enemy and the avenger.
At that time Jesus said, “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and the intelligent and have revealed them to infants;
points.apply: Choose one person who is humble and simple in your life and ask what God has taught you through them.

points.h: I was sick and you took care of me
sub: The red cross of the Camillians.
q: Do not hesitate to visit the sick, because for such deeds you will be loved.
I was naked and you gave me clothing, I was sick and you took care of me, I was in prison and you visited me.
points.apply: Visit one sick person this week, and take something small to them: a prayer, a fruit, an hour.

concl: God reveals his holiness and his compassion to a shepherd who stops to look, and promises: I will be with you.
The Father reveals himself to the little ones in Jesus, and St Camillus shows that the sickbed is holy ground.
2027-07-14.resolve: Visit one sick person this week, and pray each day: Lord, here I am.
